answer:
Most home ovens are insulated metal boxes that heat up with either gas or electricity [1]. In an electric oven, current runs through heating elements made of high-resistance wire, usually nichrome, which get hot. This is called Joule heating. The glowing elements give off infrared radiation that heats the air, the oven walls and the food [2][3]. A gas oven does the same job by burning natural gas or bottled gas at a burner, usually at the bottom of the oven [1].

A thermostat keeps the temperature steady. A sensor in the oven checks the temperature, and the controls turn the heat off when the oven reaches the setting and back on when it cools below it. That's why the element or burner cycles on and off while you cook [3][1]. The food heats in three ways: radiation from the elements and hot walls, hot air moving around it, and conduction through the pan. A convection oven adds a fan, usually at the back, that pushes the hot air around. This gets rid of hot and cold spots and usually cooks faster and more evenly [4][1]. Microwave ovens work differently: they use microwaves to heat the water molecules inside the food directly [1].
